extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of drama/literary theory (playwrights, critics, advanced literature students)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for composing and evaluating dramatic tragedy and comedy, focusing on the relation between plot and character, unity of action, conflict, idealisation, and the differences between Greek and modern drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the first principle / soul of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The plot is the first principle and as it were the soul of the tragedy.’ The plot is the animating principle of a play, the origin of movement, the starting-point and basis of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot gives the play its inner meaning and reality, is both the beginning and the end (realises the intention of the play), and contains the decisive moments (reversals and peripeteia) that most powerfully awaken tragic feeling. Without plot the play could not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethos (character) is subsidiary to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethos (the portrayal of character) holds a position subsidiary to the plot or action; character divorced from plot is like a daub of beautiful colour without form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character derives meaning and dramatic value through the medium of plot; the outline of plot corresponds to the outline of portraiture and provides form in which character gains significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama requires a connected, unified scheme of incident (unity of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be a tragedy without some kind of connected scheme of incident and situation—in a word, without a more or less unified 'action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic action must form a complete whole: a coherent series of events standing in organic relation and bound by cause and effect. Unity of action is central to the tragic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be exhibited in development and results; drama = will/emotion in action
rubrics_metrics.description: Action, to be dramatic, must be exhibited in its development and in its results; it must stand in reciprocal and causal relation to certain mental states. 'The drama, therefore, is will or emotion in action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences must see the feelings out of which deeds grow, the motives that carry actions to conclusion, and the effect of deeds upon minds — emotions generated become new factors of action and react on other characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic conflict is essential (but must have outward manifestation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama implies a conflict — a collision of forces, inward discord, or struggle with other wills — and the dramatic conflict (not mere plot) is 'the soul of the tragedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every conflict is dramatic: purely mental/internal conflicts that never manifest in outward acts are excluded unless they are brought into a plot that makes them link in a chain of events. Conflict must bring the agent into collision with other personalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only certain kinds of character are fit for dramatic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters fit for drama are of the battling, energetic type: emotions must harden into will and the will express itself in deed; passive characters suit lyrical poetry rather than drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptionally, characters like Hamlet can be dramatic through intellectual/inaction as a form of action (arrested volition). Generally, dramatic characters must have spontaneous energy to make and mould circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters are dramatic only insofar as they are grouped around the plot's centre
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are dramatic only so far as they are grouped round the centre (plot) and work with the movement of events towards an appointed end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters reveal personality only to the extent the natural course of the action requires; situations and opposing wills are chosen to elicit and test their energies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot need not be complicated; simplicity can be artistically superior
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot being primary does not imply that it must be complicated; the normal Greek tragedy is singularly simple in structure and complication for its own sake is not desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great tragedies (even Oedipus) often employ relatively simple, tightly-woven plots; the aesthetic aim is organic unity, not tangled puzzles. Excessive complication can be a vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot contains reversals and decisive moments (peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the plot which contains those Reversals of the Action (peripeteia) and other decisive moments which most powerfully awake tragic feeling and excite the pleasure appropriate to tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include well-placed reversals and decisive moments within the plot structure to produce the characteristic tragic emotions and aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner necessity / probability binds events (minimise chance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inner bond of probability or necessity binds events together; the element of chance is all but eliminated in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events should proceed from character and circumstances with a plausible causal logic so that the fate that overtakes the hero feels like the consequence of his own character ('Man's character is his destiny').

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between plot and character: reciprocal but plot-dominant artistically
rubrics_metrics.description: Though action springs from and reflects character, and the modern drama lays increased stress on character, plot remains artistically prior as the organizing principle; action and character are outcomes of each other in a completed dramatic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should ensure character development serves the unified action; modern emphasis on subjective character-development must still maintain dramatic unity and causal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation — representing the universal and embellishing the object
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry idealises life: (1) by representing the permanent and essential aspects (the universal), and (2) by heightening beauty — seizing a happy moment and ennobling it while retaining likeness to the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealisation involves suppressing accidents of individuality and enlarging particulars into the human and universal. The idealised character need not be flawless but must retain an equipoise that preserves typical human validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealised portraiture allows faults but preserves typical/higher human quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's tragic hero is not free from faults or failings; the idealising process does not imply omission of all defects — some quality(s) must be thrown into relief provided the equipoise of character is not disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroes can be morally imperfect yet rank as ideal if they possess a commanding faculty or qualities that justify their universal significance; protagonists should embody universal human elements even when flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern drama: expanded temporal scope and risk of pathologising characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern drama tends to expand the period of action and to emphasize individual/super-subjective portraiture and growth, allowing the dramatist to trace a character's evolution more completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expansion opens scope for deeper character development but carries the danger that overly reflective, introspective characters may lack the energetic will necessary for tragic action (Goethe example); beware turning dramas into dramatic biographies or pathological studies.
